summary: Extends Ethernet VPN Integrated Routing and Bridging procedures from RFC 7432 and RFC 9135 to improve mobility handling and duplicate address detection, covering more scenarios in which a host moves.

eli5.summary: When a computer moves across the network, everyone must update where to find it. This improves how the network tracks the move and spots mix-ups.

questions: how does evpn handle host mobility when ip and mac change
what is sequence number inheritance in evpn irb
subtitle: Handling host mobility when IP and MAC addresses move independently

tldr.problem: When hosts move in EVPN-IRB networks, their IP and MAC addresses do not always move together. Existing procedures assume a fixed 1:1 mapping, which breaks when an IP moves to a new MAC, or a MAC gets a new IP.
tldr.mechanism: Sequence numbers assigned to MAC routes are inherited by MAC-IP routes. When host mobility or duplicate addresses occur, this shared sequence number tracks the most recent binding across the network.
tldr.outcome: Networks can now handle three mobility scenarios: MAC+IP moving together, IP changing MAC, or MAC changing IP. Multi-homed hosts get consistent sequence numbers across all connected provider edges.

facts.label: Scenarios addressed
facts.value: 3 (MAC+IP move together, IP changes MAC, MAC changes IP)

today: RFC 9721 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2025. It extends existing EVPN-IRB implementations in RFC 7432 and RFC 9135 to support more flexible host mobility in virtualized and containerized environments.

sections.title: Introduction to EVPN-IRB Host Mobility
sections.content:
EVPN-IRB (Ethernet VPN Integrated Routing and Bridging) is a distributed network overlay that handles both Layer 2 bridging and Layer 3 routing. In standard EVPN-IRB, a single combined route carries both a MAC address and an IP address for a host, with one sequence number representing the "version" of this binding.

The existing procedures from RFC 7432 work well when a host and its IP address move together to a new location. However, virtualized environments with containerized workloads create new scenarios: a host's IP address might be reassigned with a new MAC address (such as when a VM reloads), or a MAC address might be reconfigured with a new IP address.

This RFC extends the mobility procedures to handle these cases where IP-to-MAC bindings change. It ensures that a single sequence number attribute can track the most recent reachability for both MAC and IP addresses, even when they do not move together.
sections.eli5: Normally, when a host moves, both its phone number (IP) and ID card (MAC) move together. The network already handles that. But this is about what happens when they move separately.

sections.title: The Problem: MAC-IP Address Bindings That Change
sections.content:
EVPN-IRB routes combine MAC and IP reachability in a single advertisement called RT-2 (Route Type 2). The RFC identifies three mobility scenarios that the existing procedures do not fully address:

Scenario 1: Host IP moves to a new MAC. When a host reloads or is redeployed, its IP address might persist but get a new MAC address. In data center environments with shared MAC addresses (multiple VMs on one physical server sharing the same MAC), an IP moving to a different server means a new MAC address. The existing procedure would assign this new MAC-IP binding a sequence number of 0, which does not reflect that this IP previously had a higher sequence number.

Scenario 2: Host MAC moves to a new IP. When a host is re-provisioned at the same or new location with the same MAC but a different IP address, the MAC mobility procedure in RFC 7432 would not trigger without advertising a separate MAC-only route. The new MAC-IP route would start with sequence number 0, potentially masking the fact that this MAC address has moved.

Scenario 3: Multi-homed hosts need consistent sequence numbers. When hosts are connected to multiple Provider Edge routers via an all-active multi-homed link, each PE might learn the host at different times. The independent sequence number assignments result in inconsistent advertised sequence numbers, breaking ECMP path selection and mobility procedures.
sections.eli5: The network uses sequence numbers like version numbers to know the newest location. The old way starts the version number at 0 for a new combination, even if that IP or MAC was already important somewhere else.

sections.title: Solution: Sequence Number Inheritance
sections.content:
The core innovation is sequence number inheritance. Instead of treating a combined MAC-IP route as an independent entity, it is treated as a child of its parent MAC route. The MAC-IP route inherits the sequence number from its parent MAC.

This is illustrated as: Mx-IPx ---> Mx (seq# = N), where multiple MAC-IP routes can share the same parent MAC route.

When a MAC address has multiple IP addresses (MAC address sharing), all the MAC-IP sibling routes inherit the same sequence number from the parent MAC. When an IP moves to a new MAC (Mz), the new route Mz-IPx must be assigned a sequence number higher than both the previous route (Mx-IPx) and the current Mz sequence number. This ensures that routers can determine the most recent MAC binding for the IP.

For multi-homed scenarios, local and Peer-Sync-Local routes (routes learned from multi-homing peer devices) must be kept in sync. When a route is learned locally, its sequence number is updated to be at least equal to the same route learned from a peer, preventing inconsistencies.
sections.eli5: Imagine the MAC address is the parent and the IP address is a child. All children of the same parent get the same version number. When a child moves to a new parent, it gets a number bigger than both its old parent and the new parent.

sections.title: Sequence Number Assignment Procedures
sections.content:
The RFC specifies six procedures for assigning sequence numbers correctly:

Local MAC-IP Learning: When a host's MAC and IP are learned locally via ARP or NDP, the parent MAC route's sequence number is computed to be: (1) higher than any remote MAC route for that MAC, (2) at least equal to any Peer-Sync-Local MAC route for that MAC, and (3) higher than the sequence number of any different MAC associated with that IP.

Local MAC Learning: When only the MAC is learned locally, its sequence number must be higher than remote routes and at least equal to Peer-Sync-Local versions.

Remote Route Updates: When receiving a remote MAC or MAC-IP route with a higher sequence number, all local MAC-IP routes for that MAC must be probed and deleted, triggering a re-learning procedure.

Peer-Sync-Local Updates: When receiving routes learned by a multi-homing peer device, local sequence numbers must be updated to be at least equal to the peer's values, ensuring consistency across the multi-homed interface.

MAC Address Sharing Race Condition: When simultaneous moves occur between PE devices (e.g., IP1 moves from PE1 to PE2 while IP3 moves from PE2 to PE1), proper probing ensures stale entries are removed to prevent sequence number bouncing.

Mobility Convergence: Optional ARP/NDP probing procedures can accelerate host re-learning when a MAC address appears after learning a prior remote MAC-IP route, or when a local MAC route ages out.
sections.eli5: These are the step-by-step rules for figuring out what version number to give a route. The most important one is: the new version must be higher than any previous version, no matter what name or card the host has.

sections.title: Routed Overlay and IP-Only Hosts
sections.content:
In some deployments, the overlay is purely routed: hosts are advertised only by their /32 or /128 IP prefix via EVPN Route Type 5 (RT-5), and no MAC routes are advertised at all. In this scenario, intra-subnet traffic is still IP routed at the PE rather than bridged.

The RFC applies the same mobility and sequence number procedures to IP-only routes. When a host IP is learned locally at a new PE, it is advertised with a sequence number higher than what was advertised from the old location. When a higher-sequence-number route is received, local routes with lower sequence numbers are probed and deleted.

This allows the same host mobility semantics to apply in purely routed overlays as in IRB overlays, even though no MAC route is advertised.
sections.eli5: Some networks only track the phone number (IP address) and skip the ID card (MAC). The same version number system still works for tracking when the phone number moves.

sections.title: Detecting Duplicate Hosts
sections.content:
Duplicate host detection is extended to handle the new mobility scenarios. Three duplicate scenarios are defined:

Scenario A: Same MAC, different IPs. When two hosts have the same MAC address, the existing RFC 7432 duplicate MAC detection procedure applies. All MAC-IP routes with that MAC are marked as duplicates by inheritance.

Scenario B: Same IP, different MACs. When different MAC addresses are assigned to the same IP address (misconfiguration or conflicting assignment), this is now detected as an "IP move." When learning a local MAC-IP route, if the IP is already associated with a different remote MAC, it counts as an IP move. A MAC-IP route is marked duplicate if either its parent MAC is duplicate or if its IP is detected as duplicate.

Scenario C: Same IP, no MAC route. In purely routed overlays (RT-5 only), duplicate IP detection follows MAC duplicate procedures: if the same IP is detected on multiple ESI (Ethernet Segment Identifiers), it is marked as duplicate.

Once a host is marked duplicate, corrective action must be taken to un-provision the duplicate. The RFC defines two recovery mechanisms: (1) Route Unfreezing via CLI to increment the sequence number after un-provisioning, and (2) Route Clearing via CLI to remove local entries.
sections.eli5: The network watches for mix-ups: two things with the same name or ID card. When it spots one, it marks it as a problem and stops using it until someone fixes it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations from RFC 7432 and RFC 9135 apply to this document. The extended sequence number procedures further extend consumption of sequence numbers in IRB deployments, subject to the same considerations if the control plane or data plane is compromised.

A key risk is spoofing: if the host-facing data plane is compromised, attackers could inject ARP or MAC frames claiming a host has moved, causing the legitimate host to be marked as duplicated. This could result in legitimate traffic being blackholed.

The mitigations are the same as in RFC 7432: authentication and filtering of control and data plane messages, access controls on the host-facing interfaces, and monitoring for excessive mobility or duplicate events that may indicate an attack.
sections.eli5: If someone tricks the network into thinking a host moved, the real host might stop working. The usual security practices from the base protocol still apply here.
